text:
A CPU branch predictor tries to guess which way a conditional branch will go before the branch condition is actually resolved. Modern CPUs execute instructions in a pipeline, so if they had to wait for the branch outcome, many later instructions would stall. By predicting the branch direction early, the CPU can keep fetching and executing instructions along the predicted path, maintaining high throughput.

Predictors use patterns from past branch behavior to make their guesses. Simple predictors may remember whether a branch was usually taken or not taken, while more advanced ones track a history of recent branch outcomes to detect patterns. Many CPUs also use structures like a branch target buffer to predict where a taken branch will jump, and a return address stack to predict function returns.

When the actual branch outcome is known, the CPU compares it with the prediction. If the prediction was correct, execution continues smoothly. If it was wrong, the CPU must discard work done along the wrong path and restart from

The tank fills and drains at the same time, so use the **net rate**:

\[
\text{Net rate} = 4 - 1.5 = 2.5 \text{ L/min}
\]

It starts with 20 L and holds 200 L, so it needs:

\[
200 - 20 = 180 \text{ L}
\]

Time to fill:

\[
\frac{180}{2.5} = 72 \text{ minutes}
\]

**Answer: 72 minutes**
